Bruges
broozh
n. (the decayed Flemish port whose foreign merchant colonies brought in the first Reformation books, and which remained Catholic)
Dutch Brugge, from the Old Norse bryggja or Germanic brugga, a landing stage or bridge; French Bruges.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bruges is the Flemish town where the Reformation came in by the quayside and never took the town. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries it had been the chief market of northern Europe, with permanent colonies of English, Spanish, Italian and Hanseatic merchants and their own houses and chapels; by the 1520s its channel to the sea had silted, Antwerp had taken its trade, and it was a declining city of some decayed grandeur. The foreign merchants were the opening: German and English traders brought in Lutheran books and Tyndale's New Testaments among their bales, and small conventicles met in the 1520s and 1530s. The authorities answered with the placards, and the Bruges accounts record executions for heresy through the middle of the century. No Reformed congregation of weight was ever gathered there. When Flanders divided, Bruges stayed with the king and with Rome, and it has been a Catholic town ever since. The dictionary enters Bruges as the ordinary case beside the famous ones. For every Antwerp or Ghent there were towns where the books arrived, a few men read them, some were burned, and the town went on as before, and the honest history of the Reformation includes them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as a private assembly for worship; a bale as a pack of goods; to silt as to fill with mud; and a colony as a body of people settled in a distant country.

expand to see more

CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; a secret or private assembly for religious worship, applied reproachfully.

BALE, n. A bundle or package of goods in a cloth cover, and corded for transportation.

SILT, n. Fine earth or mud deposited from running water; to fill or choke with such deposit.

COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.

DECAY, n. Gradual failure of health, strength, soundness, prosperity, or of any species of excellence.

Key Scripture

Mat 13:4 — "And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up:"

Mat 13:19 — "When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side."

1Co 3:6 — "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Modern Corruption

Decayed Flemish port whose foreign merchant colonies imported the first Reformation books, where men were executed for heresy and no Reformed church took root.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the history that only records successes, which flatters the cause and teaches nobody anything. Bruges had the books, the conventicles and the martyrs, and it has no Reformed congregation in its story; the seed fell and did not come up. The parable is plain that this is to be expected: “some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up” (Mat 13:4), and the Lord's own explanation names the agent, that the wicked one “catcheth away that which was sown in his heart” (Mat 13:19).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the labourers are not the ones who give the increase, and are therefore not the ones who are judged by it. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) covers the merchant who carried a New Testament into Bruges in a bale of cloth and saw no church come of it. The promise is not that every sowing produces a visible harvest in the sower's town, but that the word accomplishes what it was sent for: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek speiro (G4687), to sow; Greek auxano (G837), to give increase; Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word.

expand to see more

Greek speiro (G4687) — to sow, to scatter seed; “some seeds fell by the way side”, Matthew 13:4.

Greek harpazo (G726) — to snatch away by force; “catcheth away that which was sown in his heart”, Matthew 13:19.

Greek auxano (G837) — to cause to grow, to give increase; “but God gave the increase”, 1 Corinthians 3:6.

Greek phuteuo (G5452) — to plant; “I have planted, Apollos watered”, 1 Corinthians 3:6.

Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty, vainly, without effect; “it shall not return unto me void”, Isaiah 55:11.

Usage

"“some seeds fell by the way side” (Mat 13:4) — conventicles in a decayed port and no church gathered."

"“but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — Tyndale's New Testaments carried in among the bales."

"“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — executions for heresy recorded through the century."
